extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters / patent attorneys / agents involved in drafting and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for responding to office actions, amending applications (claims, description, drawings), conducting interviews, appeals, divisional/continuation filings, oppositions, issuance formalities, and broader patent strategy across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know jurisdictional timing rules and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter understands what is required in every country in which their client has pending patent applications; inquire whether the mailing date of the response or the date of office action is the date from which the time limit runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time limits and the event that starts them vary by country. Patent drafters must closely watch deadlines (e.g., US final office action six-month deadline with first three months not requiring an extension fee) and know which events suspend or extend deadlines. Missing the deadline can cause abandonment even if a reply is filed very near the date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain office-action response and counsel client choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter should explain their draft response to the office action to the client and give the client the opportunity to make choices about claim amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients may better assess business implications of narrowing claims (e.g., whether narrowed protection is still useful or can be designed around). Patent drafters should present amendment options and trade-offs so the client can decide strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter principle for amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending the application, a universal rule in most jurisdictions is that no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added (except to remedy obvious mistakes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies to claims, description, and drawings. The purpose is to balance applicants' right to amend with third parties' reliance on the original disclosure and the first-to-file principle. Drafting a complete disclosure pre-filing is therefore paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft comprehensive original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare an application with sufficiently detailed disclosure of the invention and with a proper set of claims that are a solid foundation for possible amendments later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examiners may cite prior art unknown at filing, a broad and detailed original disclosure enables permissible narrowing and amendment without introducing new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining original disclosure vs inherent disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Original disclosure covers explicit matters and also things a person skilled in the art would recognize as inherent or self-evident from the disclosure as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rely on inherent disclosure for an amendment, it typically requires that the information is necessarily present and would be readily recognized by a skilled person, not merely a possibility or probability. Demonstration must be convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example test for inherent disclosure (helical springs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application describes an apparatus mounted on resilient supports without specifying the kind of supports, adding 'helical springs' may be new matter unless it can be shown a skilled person would naturally use helical springs in that field and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use field-specific technical evidence to show a skilled person's expectation; mere speculation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying effects may not be new matter if deducible
rubrics_metrics.description: If a technical feature X is clearly disclosed but its specific effect was not fully mentioned, clarifying that effect may not be new matter if a skilled person could deduce the effect from the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the effect is necessarily present in the disclosure; if so, clarification may be permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO standard: 'directly and unambiguously derivable' test
rubrics_metrics.description: In Europe, matters not directly and unambiguously derivable by those skilled in the art from the original disclosure are considered new matter and cannot be introduced after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent drafters often file extensive multiple dependent claims and explain all possible combinations in the description to satisfy this strict standard at the EPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: US practice: incorporation by reference can form original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, a reference to another patent literature in the description (incorporation by reference) could be part of the original disclosure and thus form the basis for later amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully structure and rely on incorporations where appropriate, consistent with local rules about incorporation by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key questions when substantially amending claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending the claims substantially and limiting their scope, examiners may pay attention to: (i) unity of invention, (ii) whether amended claims are seriously inconsistent with the description (i.e., requiring description amendment), (iii) whether all amended claims are supported by the description as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before submitting substantial claim amendments, evaluate these three issues and prepare corresponding description amendments or justifications to avoid new-matter and consistency objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revising the 'problem to be solved' must be deducible from filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Revising the stated problem to emphasize an effect obtainable by the restricted claimed invention is permissible only if that emphasized effect is deducible from the application as filed by a skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invent a new problem/effect in prosecution; ensure factual/technical basis exists in original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations and disclaimers require basis in filing or special justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing negative limitations (e.g., 'excluding X') or disclaimers can raise new matter issues if the excluded subject lacks support in the application as filed; permissibility depends on jurisdiction and circumstances (e.g., to overcome accidental anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the exclusion has support or whether allowable under jurisdictional exceptions (e.g., to disclaim accidental prior art or exclude non-patentable subject matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claims and deleting features—jurisdictional constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadening a claim by removing features is permissible in many jurisdictions if no new matter is introduced, but some jurisdictions (e.g., Japan, EPO, China) prohibit deleting features consistently presented as 'essential' because deletion may introduce new technical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wording in the description that describes embodiment features as 'essential' or 'indispensable' unless necessary; evaluate local rules before attempting to broaden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding new claims during prosecution—rules differ by country
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a new claim during prosecution is generally allowed if no new matter is introduced, but some jurisdictions have special rules restricting additions (e.g., Japan prohibits claim changes that change the special technical feature after first office action; US limits substantial claim amendments after final office action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check country-specific prohibitions and timing constraints (e.g., US allows only claim deletion, examiner-requested amendments, or amendments that raise no new issue after final action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting claims allowed—prepare persuasive, clear responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to the office action with clear, concise, and persuasive arguments why claims are patentable over the cited prior art; provide proposed claim amendments where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may perform supplemental searches, reinterpret prior art, or issue further office actions if unconvinced. Responses should address the examiner's reasoning and consider the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' of claims in view of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conducting interviews with examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices allow interviews with examiners; both parties may need to submit complete and accurate written records of the interview which become part of the file history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare thoroughly (review office action and prior art), be concise and persuasive, prepare proposed claim amendments in advance, consider bringing the inventor when allowed, and counsel the inventor beforehand. Interviews can clarify examiner interpretation and facilitate agreement on amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to subsequent office actions efficiently
rubrics_metrics.description: Second and subsequent office actions should involve a narrower set of issues and, where prior art overlaps, enable quicker, more focused responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the earlier exchange to shorten subsequent prosecution; anticipate recurring issues and prepare targeted arguments or amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final office action consequences and permissible follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: A final office action may require the application to be remedied to the examiner's satisfaction, appealed, or abandoned; patent offices vary in procedures and permissible follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the US, a final office action has specific options (appeal, request for continued examination). Filing a response to a final does not itself suspend the deadline; only certain events (notice of allowance, new nonfinal action, abandonment, request for continued examination, notice of appeal) suspend the deadline. Timely management and understanding of suspension events are critical to prevent abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and administrative tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices provide administrative appeal mechanisms; appeals typically involve filing an appeal brief and may include oral hearings (e.g., US) and payment of fees; decisions may be further appealed to courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess costs, timelines, and client business interest before appealing; appeals can be to a board of administrative judges or to courts depending on jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and strategic role of divisional, continuation, and continuation-in-part applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisional applications claim part of the parent application but may retain the parent's filing/priority date; continuations repeat subject matter of the parent to pursue different claims and retain parent's filing date for disclosed subject matter; continuation-in-part (CIP) repeats substantial parts and adds new matter with different priority for added subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select divisional for pursuing withdrawn claims after restriction requirements, continuations for claim variations while keeping priority, and CIPs for claiming enhancements developed after parent filing. Understand retention of filing dates for different claim sets and jurisdictional timing rules for filing divisionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition proceedings and third-party challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may oppose patent grants (pre-grant or post-grant opposition) or seek revocation before courts; oppositions require convincing arguments (e.g., overlooked prior art showing lack of inventive step), and applicants may rebut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions can be used strategically by competitors to delay or narrow patents. Patent drafters should counsel clients that issuance is not final if opposition systems exist and should prepare opposition documents when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance formalities and post-grant maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a notice of allowance is issued, patent drafters must complete issuance formalities (pay fees, consider filing continuations) and ensure payment of periodic maintenance/annuity fees to keep patents in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Docket maintenance and clear responsibility for annuity payments (drafter, client, or third-party service) are essential. There is typically no fast way to speed printing/issuance; opposition processes may delay issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent portfolio strategy: offensive and defensive uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can be used offensively (to block, license, or litigate against competitors) or defensively (to protect against infringement suits); owning multiple patents increases bargaining power, enables cross-licensing, and makes design-arounds harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider portfolio breadth, claim quality, and complementary patents rather than relying on a single patent. Licensing strategies can start with smaller targets to build momentum rather than immediately targeting large players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional tip — pragmatic licensing approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In licensing campaigns, it is rarely a good idea to first pursue the biggest player; start with small-to-medium-sized players and build momentum toward larger ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical advice helps establish precedent and commercial momentum while reducing initial litigation/licensing resistance.
